source_text: Ὅσον δὲ ἄκριτον καὶ προπετὲς συγκατατιθεμένων τε τοῖς ἐπιτυχοῦσιν, ὁποῖα ποτ᾽ ἂν ᾖ, κἂν ψευδῆ τύχῃ καὶ ἀντιλεγόντων πολλάκις κἂν ἀληθῆ τινα εἰρημένα ᾖ. καὶ τοῦτο ἐκπαιδεύων τούτοις τε τοῖς προειρημένοις καὶ ἑτέροις ποικίλοις λόγοις. πολυειδὲς γὰρ αὐτὸ τὸ μέρος τῆς φιλοσοφίας, συνεθίζον μὴ εἰκῇ, μηδ᾽ ὡς ἔτυχε ῥίπτειν τε τὰς μαρτυρίας καὶ πάλιν ἀναδύεσθαι. ἀλλ᾽ ἐξετάζοντας ἀκριβῶς μὴ τὰ προφανῆ μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ κεκρυμμένα. πολλὰ γὰρ εὔδοξα αὐτόθεν καὶ σεμνοειδῆ, ὑπὸ εὐσχήμοσι ταῖς φωναῖς εἰσδραμόντα εἰς τὰς ἀκοὰς ἡμῶν ὡς ἀληθῆ. ὕπουλα ὄντα καὶ ψευδῆ συναρπάσαντα καὶ λαβόντα ψῆφισμα ἀληθείας παρ᾽ ἡμῶν, μετ᾽ οὐ πολὺ σαθρὰ καὶ οὐκ ἀξιόπιστα κατεφωράθη ὄντα, μάτην τὴν ἀλήθειαν ὑποκρινόμενα. καὶ ἡμᾶς εὐκόλως ἀπέφηνε καταγελάστους ἐξηπατημένους, κἀπιμαρτυρήσαντας εἰκῇ, οἷς ἥκιστα ἐχρῆν. πάλιν τε αὖ ἕτερα σεμνὰ μὲν, καὶ οὐκ ἀλαζονευόμενα μὲν, ἢ οὐκ ἀξιοπίστοις τῇ φωνῇ κείμενα παράδοξα, καὶ πάντων ἀπιστότατα δοκοῦντα, αὐτόθεν τε ἀποδοκιμασθέντα ὡς ψευδῆ, καὶ ὑβρισθέντα ἀναξίως. εἶθ᾽ ὕστερον ἐξιχνεύουσι καὶ κατανοοῦσιν ἀκριβῶς, πάντων ἀληθέστατα καὶ ἄμαχα ἀτεχνῶς εἶναι κατενοήθη, τὰ τέως ἀπόβλητα καὶ ἀδόκιμα νομισθέντα. μὴ δὴ τὰ προφανῆ μόνον καὶ προσκύπτοντα, ἔστι δ᾽ ὅτε δολερὰ καὶ σεσοφισμένα, τὰ δ᾽ ἔνδον διερευνωμένους μὲν καὶ περικρούοντας ἕκαστον, μή πῃ τι σαθρὸν ἠχήσῃ, καὶ ἐν αὐτοῖς πιστουμένους ἑαυτοὺς πρότερον, οὕτως καὶ τοῖς ἐκτὸς συνομολογεῖν καὶ ἀποφαίνεσθαι περὶ ἑκάστων ἐδίδασκεν. οὕτως μὲν τὸ περὶ τὰς λέξεις καὶ τοὺς λόγους κριτικὸν ἡμῶν τῆς ψυχῆς μέρος, λογικῶς ἐξεπαίδευεν. οὐ κατὰ τὰς καλῶν ῥητόρων κρίσεις, εἴ τι Ἑλληνικὸν ἢ βάρβαρόν ἐστι τῇ φωνῇ. τὸ μικρὸν τοῦτο καὶ οὐκ ἀναγκαῖον μάθημα· ἀλλὰ τοῦτο πᾶσιν ἀναγκαιότατον Ἕλλησί τε καὶ βαρβάροις, καὶ σοφοῖς, καὶ ἰδιώταις· καὶ ὅλως ἵνα μὴ μακρὸς εἴη μοι λόγος ἑκάστας τέχνας καὶ ἐπιτηδεύματα ἐπεξιὼν, πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις τοῖς ὁντινοῦν βίον ᾑρημένοις· εἴ γε πᾶσι τοῖς περὶ ὁτουδήποτε κοινολογουμένοις μέλει τε καὶ διεσπούδασται, μὴ ἠπατῆσθαι. καὶ μὴ τοῦθ᾽ ὅπερ εἶδος διαλεκτικὴ κατορθοῦν μόνη εἴληχε.
thought_title: Training in logic: testing every claim before assent
orientation: Origen trains them in logic, so that they test every claim before giving or refusing assent.
pass_a_gloss: And as much as [was] undiscerning and rash, of [us] assenting to things that chanced, of whatever sort they might be, even if they happened false, and often contradicting even if some things were said true; this too educating by these aforesaid and other varied arguments. For this part of philosophy itself is many-formed, accustoming [us] not at random nor as it chanced to throw the testimonies and again to draw back; but examining accurately not only the evident but also the hidden. For many things reputable at once and grave-looking, under seemly words running into our ears as true, being festering-beneath and false, having snatched and taken a vote of truth from us, after not long were detected to be rotten and not trustworthy, vainly playing the part of truth; and easily showed us laughable, deceived, and having witnessed at random to things we least ought. And again other things, grave and not boasting, or lying in untrustworthy speech, paradoxical and seeming most incredible of all, at once rejected as false and insulted unworthily; then later, to those tracking out and considering accurately (print present participles; Koetschau aorist), were perceived to be truest of all and simply irresistible, the things till then deemed castaway and spurious. Not then only the evident and peeping out, sometimes deceitful and sophisticated, but searching the things within and tapping each, lest somewhere something ring rotten, and first assuring ourselves in them, thus also to agree with those outside and to declare about each, he taught. Thus he educated logically the critical part of our soul concerned with words and arguments; not according to the judgments of fine orators, whether something is Greek or barbarous in speech, this small and unnecessary study; but this most necessary to all, Greeks and barbarians, and wise and laymen; and wholly, that my speech not be long going through each art and pursuit, to all people who have chosen any life whatever; since to all conversing about anything whatever it is a care and an earnest concern not to have been deceived. [Final sentence 'And not this only, which kind dialectic alone has been allotted to set right' rendered at section 8.]

pass_b_english: As for whatever was undiscerning and rash in us, when we gave our assent to whatever came our way, whatever it might be, even if it happened to be false, and often spoke against things even when they had been said truly, this too he schooled, both by the arguments I have mentioned and by others of many kinds. For this part of philosophy is itself many-sided, and it trains us not to cast our testimony carelessly or at random and then back out of it again, but to examine with care not only what is plain but also what is hidden. For many things that looked reputable and grave at first sight slipped into our ears as true under fine-sounding words, though they were rotten beneath and false; they carried us away and won from us a verdict that they were true, and before long they were caught out as unsound and untrustworthy, playing the part of truth in vain. Then they easily made us look ridiculous, deceived as we were, for having carelessly borne witness to what we should least of all have vouched for. And again, other things, worthy indeed and making no show, or set out in words that do not win belief, strange and seeming the least credible of all, were rejected at once as false and treated with undeserved scorn; and then later, to those who tracked them down and examined them closely, the very things that had until then been thought worthless and spurious were found to be the truest of all and simply unanswerable.

So he taught us not to search only what is plain and catches the eye, which is sometimes deceitful and sophistical, but also what is within, tapping each thing to hear whether it rings hollow anywhere, and so, having first made ourselves sure of what lies within, to give our assent to what is outside as well, and to declare our judgment on each matter. In this way he trained, by logic, the critical part of our soul that deals with words and arguments: not as the fine rhetoricians judge, whether a word is good Greek or barbarous, for that is a small and unnecessary study, but in this study, which is most necessary for all, Greeks and barbarians, learned and unlearned alike, and in short, so that I need not make a long speech by going through every art and pursuit one by one, for all people who have chosen any way of life whatever, since everyone who discusses anything at all cares about not being deceived and is in earnest about it.
notes: Overlap: the source row ends with the sentence 'Καὶ μὴ τοῦθ᾽ ὅπερ εἶδος διαλεκτικὴ κατορθοῦν μόνη εἴληχε', which is also the first sentence of section 8 (Koetschau starts chapter 8 there, and the sentence belongs grammatically to what follows). It is translated once, at the start of section 8, so readers do not meet it twice. 'Greeks and barbarians, learned and unlearned' may echo Romans 1:14 ('to Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish'), but the pairing was common and the second pair differs (ἰδιώταις, not ἀνοήτοις), so it is not cited. Tapping each thing to see whether it rings hollow is a potter's test (compare Plato, Philebus 55c, per Koetschau); not Scripture. Readings follow the print: ἀναδύεσθαι ('back out', Koetschau ἀνανεύειν 'refuse'); εὔδοξα (Koetschau ἔνδοξα, same sense); ἀλλὰ καὶ κεκρυμμένα ('but also what is hidden', which Koetschau lacks); ἐξιχνεύουσι καὶ κατανοοῦσιν (Koetschau aorists; same sense); ἐξεπαίδευεν active (Koetschau passive ἐξεπαιδεύετο; same sense). Doubtful: συγκατατιθεμένων 'gave our assent'; τοῖς ἐκτὸς (print and Koetschau) is read as neuter, 'what is outside', answering τὰ ἔνδον ('what lies within') and the καί ('as well'); a masculine reading, 'to agree with others', is possible; μὴ ἠπατῆσθαι 'not being deceived'. The opening relative clause continues the sentence begun in 7.1 (μὲν ... δέ), so it opens with 'As for'.
